title: Saving, Loading & Moving Images 📦
description: Export images to tar files, load them on another machine, and transfer without a registry.

slides.title: Why Move Images Manually? 🚚
slides.content:
# Air‑Gapped Environments

Sometimes you can’t use a registry:

- No internet access on a secure server.
- Sending an image to a colleague on a USB stick.
- Backing up a specific version of an image.

Docker provides two commands: `docker save` (export to tar) and `docker load` (import from tar).

slides.title: `docker save` — Export to Tar 💾
slides.content:
# Syntax

```bash
docker save -o output.tar IMAGE [IMAGE...]
```

- Exports one or more images into a single tar archive.
- The tar contains the layer blobs and metadata (manifest).
- You can also pipe to `gzip` for compression.

**Examples:**
```bash
docker save -o myimage.tar nginx:alpine
docker save alpine:3.18 ubuntu:22.04 -o two-images.tar

# Compressed on the fly
docker save nginx:alpine | gzip > nginx-alpine.tar.gz
```

slides.title: Save Demo 💾
slides.content: Export an Alpine image to a tar file:
slides.codeSnippet:
docker pull alpine:3.18
docker save -o alpine-3.18.tar alpine:3.18
ls -lh alpine-3.18.tar

quizData.question: What does a `docker save` tar file contain?

options.text: Only the final filesystem of the image
The image layers, metadata, and manifest
Just the Dockerfile used to build the image
A compressed snapshot of a running container

quizData.explanation: `docker save` preserves the entire image structure — layers, manifests, and tags — so it can be loaded elsewhere.

slides.title: `docker load` — Import from Tar 📥
slides.content:
# Restore Images on Another Machine

```bash
docker load -i input.tar
```

- The image (with all its original tags) is loaded into the local Docker image store.
- No network required.

**Example:**
```bash
docker load -i alpine-3.18.tar
```

You can also pipe from stdin:
```bash
docker load < alpine-3.18.tar
```

slides.title: Load & Verify ✅
slides.content: On the new machine (or after deleting the image locally to simulate), load the image:
slides.codeSnippet:
# On a different machine (or after `docker rmi alpine:3.18`)
docker load -i alpine-3.18.tar
docker images | grep alpine

quizData.question: Which command would you use to back up an image to a portable file?
quizData.explanation: `docker save` exports an image including layers. `docker export` works on containers, not images (and flattens them).

slides.title: Save vs Export Confusion ⚠️
slides.content:
## Don’t Mix Them Up

- `docker save` → works with **images** (preserves layers and history).
- `docker export` → works with **containers** (flattens the filesystem into a tar, losing layer history).

If you want to move an image, use `save`. If you want to get a flat file system snapshot of a container, use `export`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Combine Save & Load with SSH

You can transfer an image directly between machines without intermediate files:
```bash
docker save myimage:latest | ssh user@host 'docker load'
```
This pipes the tar over SSH and loads it on the remote machine in one step.
